text: — Well then, Dravichka, why are you silent, don’t you know anything about Bay Ganyo? — one of the company asked our cheerful friend Dravichka.
— How could I not know, brother, I know a whole lot of things, but how can you tell them all? — replies Dravichkata with feigned modesty.
— How will you tell them! If only I had your mouth!
— Well then, listen:

I went one summer for a trip to Genevaux, you know, in Switzerland. I took a room in a hotel and went out to walk around the city. The city was beautiful, the surroundings both picturesque and majestic. I was walking thus, aimlessly, looking left and right, and from street to street I came out onto the square where the opera house is. I see opposite me an elegant café: wait, I said to myself, let me stop in and rest a little. From the entrance on the right I see a glass partition with an open view of the square, and I go in — I’ll have coffee and watch the passersby. And what do I find there! Three whole tables occupied by Bulgarian students! Well, go and tell people that Bulgarians have no taste for elegance! In such a beautiful city, in the finest part of the city, in the most elegant café, they had taken the best place! Noise, smoke, matches and smoking cigarettes on the floor, clatter, shouting, quarrels!... Here they are playing backgammon, there prefa, beyond that trenta una!... And I hear from all sides: “Shesh-besh!... Buy!... Give the money! Jehar and ek!... Why are you looking at my cards, eh!... Garzon!... First to the second!... Dyu-besh!... You’re lying, it’s not dyubesh!... Trenta una... Spades!... Garzon!... You know nothing about prefa!... I don’t want a mind of socialists!... Dyubara!... And I don’t want a mind of the rich!... I’m trumping!... Scoundrel!... Garzon! Are you proud of the decorations?... Spades!... Well, and you with the Russian Jews? Gentlemen, the fool is coming! Ha, ha, ha!... Garzon un chope! Give me another franc on loan, eh!... You’re a swindler! Borrow from the waiter!... Dört jehar!...”

The person to whom the not entirely flattering epithet **“fool”** had been attached entered the café, greeted the students who welcomed him, as they say, with open arms, and did not know which group to join, since all the tables were trying to attract him. Such sympathy for a **fool** seemed to me at first inexplicable, but not much time passed before, from the words exchanged by the tables at this person’s expense, my bewilderment was dispelled. Then I learned that this **fool** was the son of a landowner from Argentina, in South America. A rich boy. His father sent him 500 francs a month, half of which every month was distributed, with the help of *trenta una*, into the pockets of our students. And because he good-naturedly allowed himself to be fleeced, taking pleasure in watching the curious greed with which our people lured his money from him—he was awarded the title of **fool**.

At whatever time of day I visited that café, starting from 9 in the morning until late at night, I always found the same faces engaged in the same pursuits—tables, prefa, trenta una. When these young men read, in what way they absorbed European culture—that remained unexplained to me. Only this was clear to me: that almost none of them spoke French properly. Let one of them fail to utter a word in that language, and by the roughness of the intonation, by the diction, by the construction of the phrases, you would recognize him as an Eastern man.

Every day or two, several embittered, nihilistic little Jews would join this company, snarling at the tyrant from the dark corners of the taverns. I do not know what this sympathy was for these dark heroes, who are capable at once of being nihilists, secret police agents, anarchists, and the basest sort of abusers of communal money, libraries, and other property. Instead of associating with the French, the Germans, the English—always exemplary both in their merrymaking and in their pursuits—instead of being imbued with their spirit of orderliness, diligence, honesty, and chivalry, ours found their ideal either in the little Jews, or in the little Greeks, or in certain little Armenians, who exploited their means and strength in the most despicable way, drawing them into the stifling atmosphere of their malicious, coarse, and fruitless declamations. Later I learned that in this city there were also other little Bulgarians who did not frequent this café, but were occupied most seriously with their studies.
One day, at the height of the trenta una game, when the Argentine had lost about a hundred francs, a man entered the café with a tilted cap, a staff under his arm, and saddlebags in his hand.
— Oh! Bay Ganyo! Welcome! — cried the whole company.

— Well met! How are you? — replied the newcomer, and, magnanimously declining the polite offers to make room for him around their tables, came and sat down at my table, and with his sitting overthrew my cup of coffee. A swaggering nature!
— Pardon!
— Nothing, don’t worry — I hurried to say, although I did not notice that he was worrying too much.
— Ah! Are you Bulgarian? Well, good day, what a surprise! Ganyo Balkanski! Where have you been, your grace?
I told him. We met.
— With this damned rose oil I go around the world — Bay Ganyo declared to me in a desperate voice.
— What, isn’t this trade going well?
— Well, to tell you the truth, sir, it’s not going well!
— Why is that?

— Why! We’re losing our heads over it. In the old days—if you said Bulgarian butter, they’d run like bees to honey, and now, believe that! You go into some soap shop, before you’ve even opened your mouth to say you’re Bulgarian, before you’ve even said “bonjour,” they ask you, “Essence de rose?”—and while asking, they’re smirking. But who cares about the smirk, as long as there’s some trade to be done? No, they won’t! “Give me,” he says, “one gram for a sample.” He’s mocking you! How can you give him one gram? If you pour one gram, you’ll spill two. “But, my friend,” I say to him, “this oil isn’t what you think it is, this is pure oil.” “Oh,” he says, “you all talk like that, you all sing the same song.” He says it to your face, he doesn’t want to know you at all. But still, may that damned trade at least not go to waste!... The Anatolians have eaten our heads! Why, brother, it’s not one, not two: they’ve swarmed across Europe in droves—Anatolians, Armenians, Turks, Greeks—and they lie, and they cheat people, and they burn one man, and patch up another—people are fed up! As soon as they smell rose oil—off they go looking for a bargain!...
The innocent East stood out before me with all its charms. To complete the picture, at all the tables around us, backgammon boards rattled, cards slapped — noise and smoke up to the heavens!

— I really like our boys — said Bay Ganyo to me, looking at the players. — Fine lads! There are some among them so bold that they’d put professors to shame! For example, let’s say, that boy there, the older one, do you see him? The one playing otuz-bir. Do you know that he has three medals!... For the Serbian war, for merit, and I don’t know what else. He used to be a judicial investigator, he knows the laws by heart. What did he need to keep studying for, eh—money was sticking to him! It’s been three months since he came here, but if you heard him, he speaks French like a native! Heaven forbid, he’s sharp as a tack! By now he should have become a doctor already, but the people here are stubborn. The rector, he says, won’t let him. He says it can’t be, he told him, for you to become a doctor in three months. Well, why can’t it be, when the boy knows his stuff; if you put him on the spot right now, he’ll tell you all the laws, he knows them by heart. The rector told him, it can’t be, he says, to read it all in just three months, let alone study it. Our bold one—no way, in three months I’ll be a doctor. The other one—no way, it won’t do. — Won’t do? — Won’t do! And then one day our man flared up, and when he gave him a dressing-down, he made a real fool of him... Truly, there, ask him if you want... I believed Bay Ganyo and did not go to ask the owner of the three medals.

He went on: — And do you know how this happened? It’s not enough that the rector got stubborn and won’t let the boy become a doctor, but the dean too, he says, is the same. Your Grace, you know what a “dean” is... something like, over there among them... that sort of thing... you know... Our man presented them with a whole pile of certificates — from the city council, from the prosecutor’s office, and a service record, and what not. But can you get through to a stubborn man? And it’s not, you know, some ordinary kid, but a judicial investigator! And with three medals on his chest, mind you!... The rector started droning on to him that in order to be useful to himself and to his people — what’s that got to do with him! — he ought to complete the full course regularly, that even a longer stay abroad would be beneficial for him — the fool! — and all that kind of old wives’ tales. Then leave the rector be, but — Petko and the men together — the dean speaks up too: “Yes,” he says, “and I also recommend that you listen to the rector’s advice!” Hey! And then our man’s temper flared, and he opened his mouth: “Well, why are you speaking up — are you going to become the rector’s lawyer or what!...” He blurted that out to the dean! — Those people tucked their tails between their legs, they couldn’t say a peep!... Hey, garçon! Un café!... No, whatever you say, Your Grace, but we’ve got open-hearted boys. Bravo!...
— Gerson, hey! Yun kave — shouted Bay Ganyo.
— Monsieur! — the nimble waiter replied.
— A cup of coffee and a Bulgarian newspaper — ordered Bay Ganyo, and then, turning to me, added: — I haven’t forgotten those French tricksters.
The waiter brought him coffee and some stained covers, in which several Bulgarian newspapers, torn at the edges, were clipped.

— Wait, let’s see what news there is, what’s happening in the world — said Bay Ganyo, as he opened the covers and immersed himself in politics. I watched from the side as he eagerly, with delight, devoured the brief articles, smiled, and with shining eyes let out an occasional “bravo!” After a while, overflowing, it seemed, with admiration, he turned to me:
— Oh, how they’ve smeared them! Listen, let me read it to you...
— Excuse me, Mr. Balkanski, at least here I want to give my ears a rest from this politics — I said, and got up from my chair — goodbye!
— But just listen to this: “That band of brigands of pimps, thieves, and scoundrels who stick their snouts into filth...” Wait, it gets even better later on!...
— No, no! Goodbye, Mr. Balkanski — I cried decisively and went out.
